post1.text:
Adding executives does not fix a leadership problem. It delays one.

Every week, we see companies scaling past $50M do the same thing: hire senior talent to solve organizational chaos. Strive Health recently expanded its executive team to accelerate growth in a complex industry. That move can work. But only if the leadership structure underneath is already built to carry weight.

Here is what leaders at this stage need to understand:

1. Your instinct to hire your way through a scaling crisis is usually wrong. Culture and decision rights have to be defined before new executives can operate effectively.

2. Leadership at $50M looks nothing like leadership at $200M. The skills that got you here are not the skills that will take you there.

3. Lives depend on how you lead. Not metaphorically. Your employees, their families, and your customers are all downstream of your decisions.

So before you post that C-suite job description, ask yourself this: Do you have a leadership model that will make the next hire successful, or are you just hoping they figure it out?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Stanford Graduate School of Business makes an important point: executives cannot simply drop AI into a scaling organization and expect results. They have to understand what the organization is actually ready to absorb.

At Autobahn, we see this play out constantly with companies in the $50M to $500M range. The technology is rarely the problem. Leadership readiness is. When your team lacks clear ownership, decision-making authority, and accountability structures, adding AI accelerates confusion rather than performance.

Scaling is not about adopting the right tools. It is about building the leadership foundation that lets any tool work.

If your organization is wrestling with how to lead through a growth inflection point, let us talk. post3.text:
When companies like Strive Health and Alpha Compute expand their executive teams to fuel growth, the headlines focus on the hires. What they rarely cover is whether the leadership model underneath is ready for those people to succeed.

Chapter 1 of Rock Your Business, titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It, addresses this directly. Written by Katherine Slain, the chapter challenges leaders to examine what kind of leader they are becoming as their company scales, not just who they are hiring.

One idea that stands out: the leaders who scale companies successfully are not the ones who build bigger teams. They are the ones who build leaders who can operate without them.

That shift in thinking changes everything about how you grow.

post1.text:
Your exit is not a finish line. It is a mirror that reflects every decision you made while building your company.

Most founders treat exit planning as something to handle in the final 12 months before a transaction. That is exactly backwards. The multiple you command on exit day is largely determined by choices made three to seven years earlier.

A recent Entrepreneur piece confirmed what we see constantly with clients: founders who prioritize growth rarely build the financial infrastructure, customer concentration ratios, or management depth that acquirers actually pay premiums for.

Here is what $50M+ leaders need to internalize now:

1. Recurring revenue is valued differently than project revenue. Structure your contracts accordingly, starting today.

2. Customer concentration above 20% in a single account is a silent valuation killer. Buyers discount hard for that risk.

3. A business that cannot operate without its founder is not a business. It is a job with good margins.

What would your company be worth if you were not in it?

#MergersAndAcquisitions #BusinessValuation #ExitPlanning

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes on exit planning lays out the foundational elements every business owner should address before a transaction. It is solid, practical advice. But there is a layer it does not fully explore: what makes exit planning uniquely complex for companies in the $50M to $500M range.

At that size, you are no longer a small business. But you are also not a large enterprise with dedicated M&A infrastructure. You are operating in a gap where the stakes are high and the internal expertise is often thin.

That is where the real work happens. Owners at this scale need to understand how EBITDA adjustments, management team depth, and growth trajectory all interact to shape what a buyer will actually pay.

If you are in this range and thinking about a future transaction, start the conversation now. Read the full Forbes piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPQjFIYXhibGVtZGsyVmtwMGZpTjdobTVlcEJOMURid0JybUZzRjlzc212dU85c29LdEFYMXJDRU1vNzYtVXZIZzFhZVU4T3RpdzZ5VnR2bkZ2ZXJPRG83d1hiTFJ4UF85WHR5QnNJc0wzdEdqS0xsQXdFVi1JeG0zSGxYY3ZtX1ZUYkxWaDRpcE9sTENEVlNuN1pKTkxzZmRyOGc

post3.text:
Exit planning gets plenty of general advice. What it rarely gets is a clear, actionable framework built specifically for companies already operating at scale.

Chapter 2 of Rock Your Business, titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, addresses exactly that. Written by Paul Belair and George Hohman, this chapter goes beyond the basics of valuation and gets into what sophisticated acquirers are actually looking for when they evaluate a company in the $50M to $500M range.

One thing Paul and George make clear: the gap between what a company is worth and what it could be worth is almost always fixable. But only if leadership understands where that gap lives before they go to market.

There is a specific set of value drivers that move a multiple from average to exceptional. This chapter names them.

post1.text:
Most companies don't fail at strategy. They fail at the gap between strategy and the people executing it.

Wrike recently announced a solution specifically designed to close the distance between strategic planning and real-world delivery. The market is paying attention to this problem because it's widespread and expensive.

Here's what scaling companies get wrong:

1. Strategy lives in the boardroom, execution lives in the weeds, and nobody owns the translation layer between them. At $50M+, that gap compounds fast.

2. Leaders confuse activity with progress. Having a strategic plan is not the same as having a functioning execution system.

3. Speed of implementation matters as much as quality of the plan. A decent strategy executed fast beats a brilliant strategy executed slowly almost every time.

The companies that scale from $50M to $500M are not smarter planners. They are faster, more disciplined executors who hold the line between intention and action accountable.

So here's the question worth sitting with: Who in your organization is responsible for the gap between your strategy and its execution?

post2.text:
A recent piece in HousingWire caught our attention. The National Association of Realtors is overhauling its strategic plan because leadership decided results were coming in too slowly.

That is a pattern we see constantly with scaling companies, and it rarely gets talked about honestly.

Strategic plans get written, celebrated, and then quietly ignored as daily operations take over. By the time leadership notices the results are lagging, months or quarters are already lost.

For companies between $50M and $500M, the fix is not a better plan. It is a tighter cadence of accountability tied directly to the plan's priorities.

If your strategic plan is not driving weekly decisions, it is a document, not a strategy.

Read the full article here and ask yourself how long it has been since your team reviewed your strategic priorities against actual results.

The tension between planning and execution is not a new problem. But the way you resolve it at $50M looks nothing like what it takes at $200M or $500M.

Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, titled 'What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes,' tackles this head-on. Written by Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall, the chapter draws on real operational experience across very different industries to surface a truth most leaders learn too late.

The insight that sticks: the discipline required to execute a strategy consistently is a skill that has to be built deliberately. It does not emerge naturally as a company grows. In fact, growth often makes it harder.

If your team has a strong strategic plan but weak follow-through, this chapter is going to feel uncomfortably familiar in the best way.

post1.text:
Most companies above $50M don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. Habits are what your team does by default. Strategy is what you choose deliberately, and then build systems around.

Bain recently studied B2B companies that consistently win new customers. The finding that stood out: the top performers don't just close deals differently. They systematically repeat how they find, qualify, and convert the right customers. That repeatability is the strategy. Everything else is just activity.

If you're scaling past $50M, here's what that means in practice:

1. Your sales motion needs to be documented well enough that a new hire can execute it without guessing.
2. Your ICP should eliminate prospects faster than it attracts them. Chasing the wrong deals is expensive.
3. Revenue growth is a math problem. If you can't model it, you can't manage it.

So here's the real question: if your top salesperson left tomorrow, would your sales results follow them out the door?

post2.text:
A recent piece from McKinsey on B2B growth economics makes something uncomfortable very clear: the minimum growth rate required just to stay viable has risen sharply. Companies that were coasting at modest growth five years ago are now falling behind.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is not an abstract trend. It is a pressure that shows up in lost deals, stalled pipelines, and salespeople who are busy but not productive.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. Growth stalls not because the market dried up, but because the sales strategy never matured past what worked at $10M. The market moved. The strategy didn't.

If your revenue growth feels harder than it should, that instinct is worth taking seriously. Read the McKinsey piece here and then ask yourself whether your sales approach is built for where you are now.

https://news.google.

post3.text:
Gartner just flagged something that sales leaders need to hear: AI is saving reps time, but that time is not automatically turning into revenue. Someone has to own the strategy that converts freed-up hours into closed deals.

That leadership gap is exactly what Chapter 4 of our upcoming book addresses.

In Rock Your Business, chapter authors Deb and Brandon lay out what they call the real cost of running without a sales strategy. The chapter title says it plainly: Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation.

One thing they make clear early on is that most scaling companies are not suffering from a sales effort problem. They are suffering from a sales architecture problem. Those are two very different things, and they require completely different solutions.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling someone gets when they interact with anything your company touches.

Most $50M+ companies treat branding as a design problem. It is actually an operations problem. How your sales team answers the phone, how your invoices are formatted, how a client feels after a renewal call — that is your brand.

Campari's approach to keeping legacy brands culturally relevant proves this point. Their staying power comes not from a refresh of visual identity but from deliberately connecting brand behavior to what audiences care about in real time. That is a discipline, not a campaign.

Here is what scaling companies consistently miss:

1. Brand consistency at $50M requires internal alignment, not just external messaging.
2. Your best marketing asset is the experience you deliver after the sale.
3. Culture shapes brand long before any agency does.

If every department in your company described your brand in one sentence, how many different answers would you get?

#Branding #BusinessGrowth #ScalingUp

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive featuring Ulta's CMO made something very clear: brand building and performance marketing are not two separate strategies. They are one system.

For companies scaling past $50M, this matters more than most leaders realize. At that stage, you are no longer just chasing transactions. You are building a market position that compounds over time. Ulta's approach to omnichannel shows that the companies winning long-term are the ones treating every customer touchpoint as both a brand moment and a conversion opportunity.

The mistake we see constantly in growth-stage companies is siloing brand from revenue. Marketing builds the brand. Sales closes deals. Nobody connects them.

If your marketing and sales teams cannot articulate the same value story, you have a brand problem masquerading as a pipeline problem.

Read the full article and then ask your leadership team how aligned you really are:
https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE

post3.text:
Most executives can tell you what their company does. Very few can tell you what their company feels like to a buyer who has never heard of them.

That gap is exactly what Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business tackles head-on. The chapter is called "What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?" and it is authored by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West.

The title is provocative on purpose. Smell is the sense most tied to memory and emotion. Simpson and West use it to push leaders to think about brand not as a visual exercise but as a sensory and emotional experience your market actually has with you.

One thing the chapter makes clear: at the $50M to $500M growth stage, vague branding is not a creative problem. It is a revenue problem.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost problem disguised as ambition.

SHRM's latest research on 2026 hiring trends makes this clear: the companies winning the talent game are not the ones casting the widest net. They are the ones getting ruthlessly specific about what each role actually needs to produce before they ever post a job.

For leaders scaling past $50M, three things tend to get overlooked:

1. Most job descriptions describe activity, not outcomes. If you cannot define what success looks like in 90 days, you are not ready to hire.

2. Speed-to-fill is the wrong metric. Quality-of-contribution-in-year-one is the right one.

3. Your talent bottleneck is rarely a sourcing problem. It is almost always a clarity problem at the leadership level.

The companies that scale well do not hire fast. They hire with precision, then build systems around the people they choose.

So here is the question worth sitting with: Do you actually know what your next hire needs to accomplish, or do you just know you are busy?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Yahoo Finance caught our attention: Cognizant just selected Oracle Fusion Cloud Recruiting to unify and scale its global talent acquisition operation.

For a $200B enterprise, that move makes sense. But here is what scaling companies between $50M and $500M can take from it: infrastructure decisions about talent are strategic decisions, not administrative ones.

When your hiring process is patched together with spreadsheets and gut instinct, you are not just slow. You are flying blind on the data that should be informing your next phase of growth.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders who treat their talent engine the same way they treat their revenue engine: with process, accountability, and visibility.

If your talent acquisition infrastructure has not kept pace with your growth ambitions, that is worth an honest conversation.

post3.text:
SHRM's research on precision hiring in 2026 is pointing at something our industry has danced around for years: volume-based hiring is a trap, and mid-market companies fall into it more than anyone.

Chapter 6 of Rock Your Business, titled The Talent Engine, takes this head on. Authors Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West built this chapter for leaders who know their people strategy is not keeping up with their growth rate but are not sure where the breakdown is happening.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better decisions. They make slower ones.

Most companies scaling past $50M fall into the same trap: they add metrics every quarter until the leadership team is drowning in dashboards and nobody agrees on what actually matters. Oracle NetSuite recently published a list of 30 financial metrics worth tracking in 2026. Thirty. That number alone should give pause.

Here is what high-performing companies do differently:

First, they draw a hard line between metrics that drive decisions and metrics that just describe the past. Descriptive data is not strategy.

Second, they assign ownership. A KPI with no single accountable owner is a vanity metric with extra steps.

Third, they prune. Every quarter, at least one metric should be retired. If nothing ever comes off the list, the list is not being managed.

The best-run businesses at this scale track fewer numbers with more discipline, not more numbers with good intentions.

So here is the question worth sitting with: How many of your current KPIs would your leadership team fight to keep if forced to cut half?

post2.text:
A recent piece in CLA (CliftonLarsonAllen) outlines the KPIs manufacturers should use to improve company performance. It is a solid framework for operational measurement, and worth reading if you are in that space.

But here is what it does not address: the KPI problem for companies scaling from $50M toward $500M is rarely about which metrics to track. It is about what happens when the metrics multiply faster than the team's ability to act on them.

At that growth stage, every department starts defending its own scorecard. Alignment breaks down. Leadership meetings become reporting sessions instead of decision sessions.

The fix is not a better dashboard. It is a sharper filter for what actually moves the business forward.

Read the CLA piece here and think about how many of those metrics your team could genuinely act on today: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiugFBVV95cUxNc3hGVVVxVnMwVEpLcmxaNWJzaURJbERjczZaSDhlcnhvOFlHX1VZU0tETkctQjFqRVhZVkNtcFNoUWtfSmRhSmU5N3pYc25IVzlfTEs5TjFZWk1RTmhZd2JzSkpPSXVmQndRRHRBM29CaDBoWnVWRXcxMnBhWkcwT3dmWTAwSDFSeS1hYzFtRUNtd05nWE9PX25nbzRfc2ZzSjVFVURMY0hMRkdVMmtOdjVOYUluUXJIcEE

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that carries a title most executives will recognize immediately: "Death by KPIs."

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business, authored by Héctor Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, tackles one of the most common and most costly problems companies face as they scale through the $50M to $500M range. It is not that leaders lack data. It is that they have too much of it, tracked inconsistently, owned by nobody, and reviewed too late to change anything.

One of the core ideas in that chapter is that the number of metrics a company tracks often grows in proportion to its dysfunction, not its success. More measurement is not the same as more clarity.

If your leadership team spends more time building reports than acting on them, this chapter was written for you.

post1.text:
Most companies are using AI to do the same work faster. That is not a growth strategy.

A recent report from Fast Company found that even when AI delivers real productivity gains, most CEOs cannot connect those gains to actual revenue growth. The tool is working. The strategy around it is not.

If you are running a $50M to $500M business, here is what that means for you:

1. Productivity gains that stay inside your operations are just cost savings in disguise. They do not scale the business.

2. AI needs a job description. If your leadership team cannot name exactly what decision AI is improving, it is being used as a toy, not a tool.

3. The companies pulling ahead are not using more AI. They are using it in fewer, higher-leverage places with clear accountability attached.

The question is not whether AI is working inside your company. The question is whether your leadership is working with AI in a way that actually moves the needle.

What is the one decision in your business where AI should be doing more of the heavy lifting right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune made a striking point: roughly 90 percent of executives say AI has not improved productivity at their companies, yet many are still cutting headcount in the name of AI efficiency.

That combination should concern every leader trying to scale.

At Autobahn, we work with companies in the $50M to $500M range, and this is exactly where the trap springs. Leaders adopt AI, reduce team capacity, and then discover the productivity gains they expected never materialized. Now they have fewer people and no real edge.

Growth-stage companies cannot afford to make that trade. AI has to be additive before it can be transformative.

Read the full Fortune piece and think hard about where your organization actually stands before making your next workforce or technology call.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMifEFVX3lxTE5LZWF5Vkc3Wk9DVVd5aE83ZGVhbWMyb3U3MW1kcHljOHdwcjdjTmt1SmU5bFVRblVaZGJsRndNRS1fWExxc3IyZDBJcnlxZHhYVUFhV1pBSzVRS0R1RVJlNVYxM0pzRXZKcG96RExTdTVlMnhBWDNMUlVuUGM

post3.text:
Bloomberg recently rounded up AI productivity habits from a dozen CEOs, and the range was striking. Some leaders have rewired how they work. Most are still experimenting at the edges.

Chapter 8 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles this head-on. The chapter is called The Third Monitor Theory, written by Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain, and it offers a concrete framework for how scaling companies should think about embedding AI into leadership operations, not just task lists.

One thing the chapter makes clear: the leaders who benefit most from AI are not the ones using the most tools. They are the ones who have decided exactly where human judgment still has to be in the room.

That distinction matters a lot when you are trying to grow from $50M to $500M without losing control of the business.

The leaders most likely to wreck a scaling company are not the incompetent ones. They are the ones who secretly believe they do not belong in the room.

Imposter syndrome does not disappear when revenue grows. Forbes Australia recently reported that high achievers carry self-doubt all the way to the top, and in many cases the doubt intensifies as the stakes rise. That is a real operational risk, not a feelings conversation.

Here is what that means for leaders running $50M+ organizations:

1. Unchecked self-doubt drives defensive decision-making. Leaders avoid bold moves not because the data is wrong but because they fear being exposed if it fails.

2. It creates talent gaps at the top. Executives who do not trust their own judgment will not build teams that challenge them, which kills the critical thinking a growing company needs.

3. Awareness is not the cure. Naming imposter syndrome does not neutralize it. Structured accountability and honest leadership development do.

The question worth sitting with: Is your self-doubt protecting your company or quietly limiting it?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Bona Magazine explores how executives can reframe imposter syndrome into genuine executive presence, rather than just white-knuckling through self-doubt.

It is a compelling read, and it connects to something we see consistently with companies scaling past $50 million.

At that growth stage, leadership psychology stops being a soft topic. When a CEO or senior leader is operating from a place of hidden self-doubt, it shows up in the business: slow decisions, overloaded executives who will not delegate, and cultures where no one challenges the person at the top.

The companies that scale well are led by people who have done the inner work alongside the strategic work. That combination is not accidental.

How could you build a $50 million company and still not feel like you earned the right to lead it?

That question sits at the center of Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain. The chapter is titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?" and it was written by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo.

One of the most useful things the chapter surfaces is this: imposter syndrome in scaling companies is rarely just a personal struggle. It becomes a structural problem that influences hiring, strategy, and how teams function under pressure.

The authors do not just name the pattern. They give leaders a way to work through it that is built for the pace and pressure of real growth.

post1.text:
Most leaders at $50M and above have a detailed growth plan. Almost none have a life plan.

That gap is not a personal failure. It is a structural one. The business demands everything, and the founder delivers. Until one day the business is thriving and the person running it is not.

A recent interview with wealth advisor George McReynolds highlighted what he calls the longevity trap: high-achieving professionals who optimize their companies for decades but never design the life those companies are supposed to fund.

Here is what scaling leaders rarely hear:

1. Time is the asset that does not replenish. Revenue can recover. Years cannot.
2. Defining what you are building toward personally changes how you build professionally. The decisions look different when you know what they are for.
3. Postponing life design until after the exit is a plan that almost never works the way people expect.

You have a roadmap for your business. Do you have one for your life?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur makes a point that every scaling founder should read before their next board meeting: growth planning is nearly universal among founders, but exit planning is almost nonexistent until it is too late.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly with companies in the $50M to $500M range. Leaders spend enormous energy on revenue strategy and almost none on what they actually want their life to look like on the other side of success.

The exit is not the finish line. It is a transition. And transitions without intention tend to be expensive, emotionally and financially.

If you are scaling right now, the time to think about what comes next is not after the deal closes. It is today.

post3.text:
Fortune recently ran a Morgan Stanley piece on what life actually looks like after selling a business. The central message: most entrepreneurs are unprepared for the identity shift, the loss of structure, and the question of what comes next.

This is exactly the territory Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business tackles head on.

The chapter is called Coming Up for Air, and it is authored by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain. It addresses something most business books skip entirely: how leaders at scale design a life worth building toward, not just a company worth selling.

One thing the chapter makes clear is that life planning is not a post-exit activity. It is a leadership practice. And ignoring it has real costs long before any transaction happens.
